00 Warm-up

Roll the dice, watch a bell curve appear

One die is flat: every face is equally likely. Add five together and the totals already pile up into a bell shape. That's the central limit theorem at work, and the more you roll, the closer your histogram gets to the exact distribution.

01 About

From formal proofs to data that persuades

↖ so is yours

Divergence to infinity, one quantifier at a time

I'm a mathematician with a background in statistics. It started with linear algebra, which I loved long before I understood where it would take me: into deep learning, machine learning, and most corners of applied statistics.

Statistics is what pulled me in properly. It's the discipline that lets you take a pile of numbers and turn it into an argument: prove an idea, solve a problem, or predict something before it happens.

That's the part I couldn't walk away from. So now I split my time between the pure and the applied: doing the mathematics properly, then putting it to work in real data, across whatever field will have it.

001 · Schrödinger pitch control

Pitch control assumes we can see all 22 players.

William Spearman's model (MIT Sloan, 2018) asks which team would win the ball at every point on the pitch, from how fast each player could get there.

Broadcast cameras can't. 40.7% of player-frames are off screen.

The camera follows the ball. Everyone outside its view, the hollow rings, has to be estimated rather than measured.

So each unseen player becomes a distribution, not a point.

Averaging over where they could be moves a median of 166 m² of control per frame, and the spread shows where the answer is genuinely uncertain.

Now try it yourself.

Drag any player and the surface reshapes. Switch between plug-in, expected and spread.

001SkillCorner Analytics Cup

Schrödinger pitch control

William Spearman's pitch control model (MIT Sloan, 2018) asks which team would win the ball at every point on the pitch, and assumes every player can be seen. Broadcast tracking can't. I replaced each unseen player with a calibrated probability distribution and measured how much that moves control. Whether it predicts passes better is inconclusive on one match, and the write-up says so.

002Shipped

Adversarial robustness of CNNs

A VGG-style CNN on CIFAR-10, attacked with FGSM and PGD to test whether adversarial vulnerability follows from the piecewise-linear geometry of ReLU networks.

003Shipped, live app

F1 telemetry and strategy dashboard

A Streamlit app on FastF1 data. It estimates overtake odds by simulation, updates driver pace with a Bayesian conjugate prior built from practice sessions, and backtests a gradient boosting position predictor.

004Shipped

Forecasting Beijing air quality

Prophet forecasts of daily PM2.5 in R. A custom Lunar New Year effect captures the firework spikes, then a log transform handles the heteroscedastic winter variance so the prediction intervals stay honest.

Chapter 05

Quantum and chips

The hardware side of computing: electrical engineering, semiconductors and quantum computing. Quantum computing is linear algebra made physical. A qubit is a unit vector, every gate is a unitary matrix, and measuring it is pure probability.

For now it is what I read about rather than build. That is the next chapter.
